It’s maybe a sign of how the chain’s going, though. I last shopped there a few weeks ago – picking up a gift voucher for K’s niece – and it was a strange experience. Because my local Woolworths doesn’t seem to have changed for a long, long time. Everyone else on the high street has shiny displays; Woolworth’s here is a step back in time. Slightly worn shelving that wouldn’t have looked out of place in my grandfather’s newsagents twenty-five years ago; everything piled up on it without much thought. Worn linoleum. No fancy ceiling or light fittings: bare plaster and unshaded fluorescent tubes are fine for Woolworths. If the shelves had been emptier, I’d have thought maybe a wormhole had decanted me into Moscow, circa the Andropov years. I almost expected to find carrier bags bearing the 70s coil-of-wool logo that I remember from childhood.
Personally, I still have a little bit of affection for the place. I’d never shop there, not any more, but once upon a time I did. Back when I was a teenager, it was the first place I ever bought music from; my first port of call at first; and then, as I knew more, the place I would come to flick through the 7″ singles and buy ones that had just dropped out of the charts. When they stopped selling vinyl, in about ’95 or so, I stopped going.
I almost typed there: “if you told a teenager today that Woolworths…” – and then I stopped and deleted it, because it made me feel old. Strange to think, though, that people today have completely forgotten Woolworths was once the best place to buy singles, back when Apple were a failing computer company** and portable music meant songs taped off the radio. Nowadays, it isn’t the best place to buy anything. Still stocking vinyl would hardly help, in this decade, but looking a bit smarter might. If they didn’t look like they’d furnished the place with other people’s cast-off shelves, it would be a start.
* A bit different to when the Fopp/Music Zone chain fell over: one day they stopped taking card payments, the next the shops didn’t open, and that, then, was that. Or, indeed, the Dutch ISP Aramiska, which gave its customers a few hour’s warning before they ceased operating with no explanation.
** People forget today that the first Apple Mac was a commercial disaster, so much so that its champion, Steve Jobs, got fired from the company partly as a result. I recommend reading any of the many books about the development of the Mac and the Apple company in the early 80s.

Blues music has its roots in African American communities in the Southern United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Originally a form of folk music, blues was characterized by its simple melodies, repetitive chord progressions, and emotive lyrics about love, loss, and hardship. Some of the most influential blues artists include:

1. Robert Johnson - A legendary guitarist and songwriter who only recorded a handful of songs in his lifetime, Robert Johnson is considered one of the most influential blues artists of all time. His dark and emotive lyrics, coupled with his virtuosic guitar playing, have inspired generations of musicians.

2. Muddy Waters - Often credited with popularizing electric blues music, Muddy Waters' gritty vocals and electrifying guitar playing helped shape the sound of modern blues. He was a major influence on many rock musicians, including the Rolling Stones and Eric Clapton.

3. B.B. King - Known for his soulful vocals and emotive guitar playing, B.B. King is often referred to as "The King of the Blues." He was a major influence on a wide range of musicians, including Jimi Hendrix, Stevie Ray Vaughan, and Eric Clapton.

Rock music, on the other hand, emerged in the United States in the 1950s, as a fusion of blues, country, and other forms of popular music. It quickly became a worldwide phenomenon, with artists from all over the world embracing the genre and pushing its sonic boundaries. Some of the most influential rock artists include:

1. Elvis Presley - Often cited as the "King of Rock and Roll," Elvis Presley's electrifying performances and signature sound helped shape the early sound of rock music. Songs like "Jailhouse Rock" and "Hound Dog" are now considered classics of the genre.

2. The Beatles - One of the most influential bands of all time, The Beatles revolutionized rock music with their innovative songwriting, catchy melodies, and intricate harmonies. Their albums like "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band" and "Abbey Road" are now considered landmarks in the history of rock music.

3. Jimi Hendrix - Known for his innovative guitar techniques and visionary songwriting, Jimi Hendrix helped redefine the sound of rock music in the late '60s. Hits like "Purple Haze" and "All Along the Watchtower" are now considered classics of the genre.

Generate according to: I was lucky to have had great creative writing teachers when I was in high school. They were very passionate about literature, and because of them I continued to pursue creative writing. Those teachers also impacted me because of the great creative writing activities they used to allow the imagination to run free.
Here are some creative writing activities and prompts that will honor your students’ imaginations. Let them free their muses to soar.
Free Writing—5 minutes to write on a “spark word” determined by the teacher. Then pair and share.
Flying Balls—Bouncy Castle balls with an opening sentence written on each. Toss a random one to a student who continues the “ball rolling” with a further thought or another sentence on the first. The ball is then tossed to another student who does the same.
Modelling—Show them examples of good, interesting writing. Key in on students’ interests.
Character—Show random pictures of people from the Internet. Develop a character from the image using prompt questions provided by the teacher.
Skills Lessons—Teach writer’s craft elements in chunks and focus on specific ones at a time. Examples are dialogue, developing setting, conflict, narrative point of view, etc.
Music—Play low-volume atmospheric instrumental background music while students are working.
Learning Outcome and Success Criteria—Helping them know and understand the goal or outcome they are striving for and where they are going allows them to stay focused.
Life is Not Like a Box of Chocolates: Use the prompt: “Life is like a box of…” You fill in the blank and go from there.
No-Send Letters: If you know you’ll never send a letter to someone of your choice, what would you write on it?
Raising Voices: Teacher creates character names, ages, and occupations, and assigns one character to each student. They create a monologue for that character.
Mixing Up Metaphors: Brainstorm overused metaphor phrases. Replace the last word of each metaphor with something creative and unexpected.
Found Poetry: Camera scavenger hunt around the campus—locate signs, labels, notes, words and snap pictures. Compile pictures in class and compose poetry (or create a collage) using only those words.
Teachers who display an infectious passion for great creative writing can inspire us to great heights. They will know how to tap into students’ genius. content:Speaker assistant says: Touring as a musician is both exhilarating and exhausting. It involves a lot of hard work, long hours, and endless travel, but it also provides the opportunity to perform in front of fans, connect with fellow musicians, and explore new locations. Here is a detailed account of what it's like to be a musician on tour:

Pre-tour Preparation:

Before embarking on a tour, it is essential to have a well-planned itinerary that includes all the dates, venues, and travel arrangements. This is usually handled by the tour manager and the booking agent. The musicians need to pack their gear and instruments carefully and make sure everything is in working condition before hitting the road. They also need to rehearse their setlist, which can involve several hours of practice every day. Some musicians may also need to engage in vocal exercises or take care of their instruments' maintenance to ensure they are in optimal condition throughout the tour.

Daily Routine:

A typical day for a touring musician usually commences early in the morning. They may grab some breakfast at the hotel or venue and then head out to the next location. This can involve a long drive or a flight to the next city. During the commute, musicians often catch up on rest or work on their music.

Once they arrive at the next venue, the musicians will begin set up and soundcheck, which can take a few hours. They will then have a bit of downtime to eat and relax before the show. If the venue allows, some musicians may meet fans, sign autographs or take photos with them. This is usually followed by a pre-show routine, which can involve drinking tea, vocal warm-ups, or stretching exercises.

Challenges:

Touring can be challenging for musicians. They spend much of their time away from home, and it can be challenging to maintain a healthy lifestyle on the road. This can include struggling to find healthy food options, getting enough rest, and missing loved ones. Moreover, travelling can be unpredictable with flight delays, traffic, or random changes in the itinerary. Musicians must have a clear and positive mindset and be ready to overcome these challenges.

Interactions:

On tour, musicians spend a lot of time with their team, including managers, road crew, and sound technicians. There is often a good level of camaraderie among them because they're all in the same boat. Musicians also interact with fans, which is one of the most satisfying facets of touring. Fans often appreciate meeting their idols in person, and musicians enjoy the opportunity to hear their feedback directly. Additionally, musicians can make lifelong friendships with other artists on tour.

Technical Requirements:

Touring musicians need to be technically proficient to make the best of their abilities on stage. This can include setting up instruments correctly, getting the sound correct with the venue's sound system, or fine-tuning their band's cohesion and chemistry. Some musicians have specialized requirements, such as particular microphones or amplifiers that they prefer to use.

Impromptu Performances and Events:

Occasionally, during the tour, opportunities for impromptu events or performances arise. These may include radio interviews, press conferences, or even spur-of-the-moment jam sessions with their fellow touring musicians. The musicians must be flexible and open to change, as these types of scenarios can come up unexpectedly.

Conclusion:

Touring is a unique experience that, while demanding, can also be the opportunity of a lifetime for many musicians. It requires dedication, hard work, and a love of performing, but those who decide to take on the challenge often reap the benefits. From the daily routine to technical requirements and unexpected events, touring creates memories that musicians will cherish for the rest of their lives. context:Musician travels on tour - daily routine and challenges keywords: touring, musician, tour, preparation, routine, challenges, teamwork, performance, travel, equipment, soundcheck, fans, improvisation. tags: tour, musician, travel, experience

These can include transportation costs (such as flights or bus rentals), hotel accommodations, food, and equipment maintenance. Often, the musicians will work with their manager or tour accountant to keep track of these expenses and ensure that they stay within budget. Revenue:

There are several ways that musicians can make money on tour. The most obvious is through ticket sales, where a percentage of the revenue goes to the artist. Merchandise sales like T-shirts, posters, and CD's are a significant source of revenue. VIP packages, where fans pay a premium for a meet-and-greet or other exclusive event, can be valuable as well.

Keeping Track of Finances:

Artists typically work with a tour accountant or manager to keep track of finances. content:Speaker assistant says: Sure! The fisheye representation and compact overviews are designed to work together in a complementary way to help users navigate through their calendars and perform complex tasks. 

The fisheye representation is a technique that was developed specifically for small handheld devices such as PDAs. It allows users to see more detail in a smaller space by magnifying the important information while minimizing the less important information. This technique works by zooming in on the selected date while simultaneously shrinking the surrounding dates, making it easier for users to focus on the relevant events while maintaining an overview of their entire calendar.

The compact overviews, on the other hand, provide users with a broader picture of their calendar. They allow users to see multiple months at once, giving them an overview of their schedule for the upcoming weeks and months. This feature makes it easier for users to plan their activities over a longer period of time, such as scheduling appointments and meetings, setting deadlines, or tracking project timelines.

Together, these two techniques enable users to navigate their calendars efficiently and perform complex tasks with ease.
